title: Baby Fever: When to Worry and What to Do
summary: A baby fever is a rectal temperature of 100.4°F or higher. See when to worry by age, how to take your baby's temperature, which fever medicines are safe, home care tips, and when to call the doctor or go to the ER.
body_markdown:
A fever in a baby is a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Most come from common viral illnesses and clear up in 2 or 3 days - a fever is a sign your baby's body is fighting infection, not an illness itself. How your baby looks and acts matters more than the number. The one big exception is age: if your baby is under 3 months old, any fever needs a doctor right away.


Baby 3 months or older with a fever? Message a Blueberry pediatrician or pediatric nurse practitioner anytime, day or night.


[Start a visit](https://app.blueberrypediatrics.com/bbjoin?show_monthly_kit_30=true)


## Key Takeaways


- A fever in a baby is a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. A normal temperature runs about 97.5°F to 99.5°F. Under the arm, 99°F (37.2°C) or higher may be a fever and should be rechecked with a more accurate method (under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away instead).
- If your baby is under 3 months old, any fever needs a doctor right away - even if your baby seems fine. Don't give fever medicine first.
- Watch how your baby looks and acts, not just the number. A baby who drinks, plays, and perks up after fever medicine is usually a good sign.
- Rectal is the most accurate way to take a baby's temperature, and the best choice under 3 months. A digital forehead thermometer is next best.
- Most baby fevers are viral and last 2 or 3 days. Fever medicine is for comfort, not to cure the illness or force the temperature to normal.
- Febrile seizures (seizures brought on by a fever) look scary but are almost always harmless. Call 911 if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.
- Go to the ER or call 911 for any emergency sign, such as being hard to wake, trouble breathing, a stiff neck, or purple spots on the skin.


## What Counts as a Fever in a Baby?


A baby has a fever when a rectal temperature reads 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. This is the number pediatricians use at every age.


A normal baby temperature isn't a single number - it runs about 97.5°F to 99.5°F (36.4°C to 37.5°C). It's lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon, so a reading that looks a little high at 5 p.m. may be normal.


A few everyday things can nudge the number up without a true fever: being overdressed or bundled, a warm room, or active play. For baseline numbers, see our guide to a baby's normal temperature and when it's a fever.


## How Do I Take My Baby's Temperature Accurately?


For babies, a rectal (bottom) reading is the most accurate, and it is the best choice for babies under 3 months old.


Here is how to take a rectal temperature safely:


- Clean the thermometer tip with soap and water or rubbing alcohol before and after each use.
- Put a small amount of petroleum jelly on the tip.
- Lay your baby face down on your lap, or on their back with the legs pulled up toward the chest.
- Gently slide the thermometer about half an inch into the anus (up to 1 inch for babies 6 months and older). It should go in easily. Stop if you feel any resistance.
- Hold it in place until it beeps, then read the number.


Other thermometers each have their place:


- A digital forehead (temporal artery) thermometer is the next most accurate after rectal, and you can use it at any age. For babies under 3 months, rectal is still best.
- An armpit reading is the least accurate, but you can use it to screen a baby of any age. Under the arm, 99°F (37.2°C) or higher may be a fever and should be rechecked with a more accurate method, like a rectal or forehead thermometer. For babies under 3 months, see the warning below.
- Ear thermometers are not reliable for babies under 6 months, whose ear canals are too narrow.
- Forehead strips and pacifier thermometers are not accurate. Skip them.


Under 3 months? Act on the first fever reading


For babies under 3 months, use a rectal thermometer. But if a forehead thermometer shows 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, or an armpit reading is 99°F (37.2°C) or higher, call your pediatrician right away. Don't wait to confirm it with a second reading.


## Baby Fever by Age: What's Normal and When to Worry


At every age, a fever starts at 100.4°F (38°C), rectal. What changes with age is how quickly you should call. The younger your baby, the lower the bar for picking up the phone. Is a fever in a baby dangerous? On its own, usually not - what matters is your baby's age and how they look and act.


Under 3 months old? Any fever is urgent


A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher needs a doctor right away, even if your baby seems fine. Call your pediatrician now. They may send you to the ER. If you can't reach them within a few minutes, go straight to the ER. Don't give fever medicine first.


A baby this young needs to be checked in person, so this is not a fever for a virtual visit. For the full details, see our[newborn fever guide](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/newborn-fever-when-to-worry-pediatricians-guide) .


### Baby Fever by Age: A Quick-Reference Table


Use this baby fever chart as a quick guide. The numbers are rectal or forehead readings. Under the arm, 99°F (37.2°C) or higher may be a fever, so recheck with a more accurate method - or, if your baby is under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away. If your baby ever looks very sick, trust that over any number.


Your baby's age A fever is… Call your pediatrician Go to the ER or call 911


Under 3 months (12 weeks) 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, rectal Right away, for any fever, even if your baby seems fine. Don't give fever medicine before your baby is seen. If you can't reach your pediatrician within a few minutes, or if any emergency sign is present


3 to 6 months 100.4°F (38°C) or higher For any fever, call within 24 hours. At 101°F (38.3°C) or higher, call now. Any emergency sign


6 to 24 months 100.4°F (38°C) or higher At 103°F (39.4°C) or higher. If a fever lasts more than 24 hours. Right away if the fever keeps going above 104°F (40°C). Any emergency sign


2 years and older 100.4°F (38°C) or higher If a fever lasts more than 3 days (72 hours). Right away if the fever keeps going above 104°F (40°C). Any emergency sign


At any age, call your pediatrician right away if your baby has a fever and:


- Looks very sick, is unusually drowsy, or very fussy
- Was in a very hot place, like a hot car
- Shows signs of dehydration
- Has had a seizure
- Has a health problem that weakens the immune system


At any age, go to the ER or call 911 if your baby:


- Can't be woken or is hard to wake
- Has severe trouble breathing
- Has purple or blood-colored spots on the skin
- Has a stiff neck
- Has a bulging soft spot
- Has a seizure
- Isn't alert when awake


### Is 100°F, 101°F, 103°F, or 105°F a Fever in a Baby?


Here are quick answers to the exact temperatures parents search for most.


Is 99.5°F a fever in a baby? No. For a rectal, forehead, or ear reading, 99.5°F is the top of normal. Under the arm, 99°F or higher may be a fever and should be rechecked with a more accurate method. Under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away instead.


Is 100°F a fever in a baby? Not by a rectal reading. A fever starts at 100.4°F (38°C). Under the arm, 100°F may be a fever, because armpit readings run lower than the true temperature. Recheck with a more accurate method, like a rectal thermometer - or, if your baby is under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away.


Is 100.4°F a fever? Yes. 100.4°F (38°C) is where a fever starts. If your baby is under 3 months old, call your pediatrician right away.


Is 101°F a fever in a baby? Yes. Under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away. At 3 to 6 months, call your pediatrician. An older baby who is drinking and playing can usually rest at home.


Is 102°F a fever in a baby? Yes. It's a common fever with viruses and isn't harmful by itself. Fever medicine can help if your baby is uncomfortable. (For a baby under 3 months, the "call right away" rule above still comes first.)


Is 103°F dangerous for a baby? It isn't dangerous by itself, but call your pediatrician. How your baby looks and acts tells you more than the number does.


Is 104°F too high for a baby? It's a high fever, so call your pediatrician now. It won't harm the brain, but a fever this high needs a doctor's advice.


Is 105°F an emergency? Call your pediatrician now. Fevers this high are uncommon. If your baby was in a hot car or a hot room, call 911 - that can be heatstroke.


## What Causes a Fever in Babies?


The most common baby fever causes are viral infections. These include colds, the flu, RSV, roseola, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and stomach bugs.


Fevers from viruses usually run between 101°F and 104°F (38.4°C and 40°C) and last 2 or 3 days, per[HealthyChildren.org's symptom checker](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/tips-tools/symptom-checker/Pages/symptomviewer.aspx?symptom=Fever) . They aren't harmful on their own.


Less often, a fever comes from a bacterial infection. In young babies, a urinary tract infection is the most common serious one, and a fever may be the only sign. Ear infections, pneumonia, and (rarely)[meningitis](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/head-neck-nervous-system/Pages/Meningitis.aspx) are also possible - that's why the warning signs below matter.


Teething can cause a slight rise in temperature within the normal range, but research shows it does not cause a true fever of 100.4°F or higher. For more, see our guide to[teething and fever](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/teething-fever) .


Fever after shots is common. It usually starts within a day and goes away in 1 to 3 days. After the MMR and chickenpox shots, a fever can show up 1 to 4 weeks later. If your baby is under 3 months old, call your pediatrician right away for any fever, even after shots.


## When Should I Call 911 or Go to the ER?


Some warning signs mean your baby needs emergency care now - not a phone call or a wait-and-see. Trust these signs over any temperature reading.


Call 911 or go to the ER now if your baby


Can't be woken up or is very hard to wake; has severe trouble breathing (grunting, flaring nostrils, pulling in at the ribs, or blue lips); has purple or blood-colored spots or dots on the skin; has a stiff neck; has a bulging or swollen soft spot; has a seizure; is too weak or floppy to move normally; or isn't alert when awake.


Call your pediatrician right away (this is urgent, but usually not a 911 call) if your baby has a fever and:


- Is under 3 months old and has any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. If you can't reach your pediatrician within a few minutes, go to the ER.
- Looks very sick, is unusually drowsy, or is very fussy and hard to calm
- Was in a very hot place, like a hot car (this can be heatstroke - call 911 if your baby is very hot and not acting right)
- Has signs of dehydration: no wet diaper in more than 8 hours or far fewer wet diapers than usual, a very dry mouth, no tears, or a sunken soft spot
- Has had a seizure
- Has a health problem that weakens the immune system
- Has repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- Has an unexplained rash


Call your pediatrician (during regular hours is usually fine) if:


- A fever lasts more than 24 hours in a baby 3 months to 2 years old
- A fever lasts more than 3 days in a child 2 years or older
- The fever goes away for a day and then comes back


Febrile seizures: any baby who has a seizure with a fever should be seen. Call 911 if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or your baby has trouble breathing.


Baby 3 months or older, with a fever but no emergency signs? Talk with a Blueberry pediatrician or pediatric nurse practitioner right away.


## My Baby Has a Fever and Seems Unusually Sleepy or Fussy - Is That Normal?


Baby fever and lethargic, or just sleepy? Some sleepiness and fussiness is normal, because fighting an infection takes energy. Most babies perk up once the fever comes down. True lethargy is different: a baby who is hard to wake, floppy, or not alert when awake needs emergency care.


The best check is how your baby acts after fever medicine has had an hour or two to work. A baby who wakes up, looks at you, feeds, and plays a little is a good sign.


Call your pediatrician right away if your baby:


- Still seems very sick after the fever comes down
- Is unusually drowsy, or very fussy and hard to calm
- Cries nonstop, or cries when touched or moved


Go to the ER or call 911 if your baby:


- Is hard to wake up, or you can't wake them
- Is floppy or too weak to move normally
- Isn't alert when awake


Under 3 months? Don't wait to see how your baby acts. Call right away for any fever.


## What Medications Can I Give My Baby for a Fever?


Fever medicine is for comfort. It doesn't cure the infection or need to bring the temperature all the way to normal. If your baby is drinking and resting comfortably, you may not need it at all.


Acetaminophen (Tylenol) can be used from 3 months, and ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil) from 6 months. For babies under 2, ask your pediatrician for the right dose.


- Your pediatrician will give you a dose based on your baby's weight. You can repeat acetaminophen every 4 hours if needed. Don't give more than 5 doses in 24 hours.
- For ibuprofen, repeat every 6 to 8 hours if needed. Don't give more than 4 doses in a day.
- Never give acetaminophen to a baby under 3 months without your doctor's approval.


For a step-by-step dosing chart, see our[baby Tylenol dosing guide](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/baby-tylenol-dosing-guide) .


Never give a baby or child aspirin


Aspirin can cause Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness that causes sudden swelling in the brain and affects the blood and liver. Never give aspirin to a baby or child with a fever or viral illness.


Can I alternate acetaminophen and ibuprofen? Some doctors have parents switch between the two, but the AAP advises caution: juggling two medicines makes dosing mistakes and accidental overdose more likely. One large review found using both brought fevers down faster than acetaminophen alone over the first 4 to 6 hours, but it didn't look past 6 hours. Only alternate on a schedule your pediatrician gives you.


One more note: don't give fever medicine around the time of shots just to prevent a fever. In one study, babies who did had a weaker immune response to several vaccines. If your baby is under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away for any fever after shots. Don't give fever medicine first. For an older baby, a mild fever after shots (100°F to 102°F) doesn't need medicine. For a higher fever, fever medicine can help.


## How Do I Care for My Baby at Home With a Fever?


Home care is mostly about keeping your baby comfortable and hydrated while their body does the work.


- Fluids. Keep offering breast milk or formula. Under 6 months, that is all your baby needs - no water. From 6 months, you can add small sips of water or an oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte.
- Dress lightly. One light layer of clothing is best. If your baby is shivering or has chills, add a light layer or a wearable blanket (sleep sack), not a loose blanket.
- Cool them down gently. If your baby is overdressed or in a warm room, remove a layer and move to a cooler spot. If your baby is under 3 months, don't wait to recheck - call your pediatrician.
- Rest. Let your baby sleep as needed. Sleep helps the body fight infection.


Don't use alcohol rubs, ice, or cold baths


Old remedies like rubbing alcohol, ice packs, or cold baths are no longer recommended to bring a fever down. They can actually cause harm. Stick to a light layer, fluids, and rest.


For help keeping your baby comfortable overnight, see our guide to[dressing a baby with a fever at night](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/how-to-dress-baby-with-fever-at-night) .


## What Are Febrile Seizures, and Should I Worry?


A febrile seizure is a seizure brought on by a fever, usually in children between 6 months and 5 years old. They happen in about 3 or 4 of every 100 children and look frightening, but they're almost always harmless and cause no lasting damage.


Most are "simple": under 15 minutes, not repeated within 24 hours, and involving the whole body. A "complex" seizure lasts longer, happens more than once in a day, or affects only one side. Most stop on their own within 1 or 2 minutes.


If your baby has a febrile seizure:


- Lay them on their side on a safe surface, away from hard or sharp objects.
- Turn their head to the side so any spit-up can drain out.
- Do not put anything in their mouth. Your baby will not swallow their tongue.
- Don't hold them down. Time how long the seizure lasts.
- Call 911 if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.


Call your child's doctor after any febrile seizure, even a short one.


Fever medicine does not prevent febrile seizures


Giving acetaminophen or ibuprofen can lower a fever, but it does not stop a febrile seizure from happening. Don't give extra fever medicine hoping to prevent one.


A few facts for perspective: simple febrile seizures don't cause brain damage or learning problems, and only a very small number of children who have them go on to develop epilepsy. About 1 in 3 who have one will have another, and they tend to run in families.


## Common Baby Fever Myths, Debunked


Fever worries a lot of parents. Here are the facts behind the most common myths.


"A fever will hurt my baby's brain." The fever itself does not harm your baby's brain. Fevers above 106°F (41.1°C) are rare. Some serious infections, like meningitis, can harm the brain - that's why the warning signs above matter, not the number itself.


"I have to 'break' the fever." You don't. A baby who is drinking and playing is often fine without any medicine. Treat for comfort, not for the number.


"Teething causes a high fever." No - teething can cause a slight rise within the normal range, but not a true fever of 100.4°F or higher.


"A higher number means a sicker baby." Not always. A baby with a 101°F fever can be sicker than a baby with 103°F. How your baby looks and acts is the better guide.


## When Should I Start a Blueberry Visit for My Baby's Fever?


For a fever that is not an emergency, a Blueberry visit can help you decide what to do next - often from your own couch.


With Blueberry Pediatrics, you get 24/7 access to board-certified pediatricians or pediatric nurse practitioners from home. Our team can review your baby's symptoms, guide you on home care and medicine, and help you decide whether your baby needs to be seen in person. In our telehealth fever visits, the most common question parents ask is what to do when their baby's temperature is in the 100–101°F range.


For babies 3 months and older without emergency signs, a quick virtual visit can save you an unnecessary trip to urgent care or the ER. It is not a replacement for emergency care.


Blueberry is not for emergencies or young-baby fevers


If your baby is under 3 months old with any fever, or has any emergency sign above, call your pediatrician right away or go to the ER - don't wait for a virtual visit.


Have a fever question about a baby 3 months or older? Message a Blueberry pediatrician or pediatric nurse practitioner anytime.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Baby Fever


### What temperature counts as a fever in a baby?


A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher. Under the arm, 99°F or higher may be a fever and should be rechecked with a more accurate method, like a rectal thermometer. If your baby is under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away instead of rechecking.


### How do I take my baby's temperature accurately?


Rectal is the most accurate, especially under 3 months. A digital forehead thermometer is the next best. An armpit reading can screen at any age, but 99°F (37.2°C) or higher may be a fever and should be rechecked with a more accurate method (under 3 months, call your pediatrician right away). Don't use ear thermometers under 6 months, and skip forehead strips.


### Is a low-grade fever (100 to 102°F) something to worry about?


Usually not after 3 months. A low-grade fever helps the body fight infection. Under 3 months, any fever needs a doctor right away. At 3 to 6 months, call your pediatrician.


### What's a high or dangerous fever in a baby?


Above 104°F, call your pediatrician now. Under 3 months, any fever of 100.4°F or higher needs a doctor right away. The fever itself doesn't harm the brain, and fevers above 106°F are rare. Heatstroke, from being in a hot place, is an emergency.


### What causes most baby fevers?


Viral infections like colds, the flu, RSV, roseola, and stomach bugs. Less often, bacterial infections such as urinary tract infections and ear infections.


### When should I call the pediatrician versus go to the ER?


Use the age table and emergency-sign list above. Any emergency sign, like trouble breathing or being hard to wake, means the ER or 911.


### My baby has a fever and is unusually sleepy or fussy - is that normal?


Some is normal. Judge by how your baby acts once the fever comes down. If your baby is under 3 months, don't wait - call right away for any fever. If your baby is hard to wake, floppy, or not alert, get emergency care.


### What medication can I give my baby, and at what age?


Acetaminophen from 3 months, ibuprofen from 6 months. For babies under 2, ask your pediatrician for the dose. Never give aspirin.


### Can I alternate acetaminophen and ibuprofen?


Only on a schedule your pediatrician gives you. The AAP advises caution, because switching between two medicines raises the risk of dosing mistakes.


### How do I care for my baby at home with a fever?


Offer fluids (only breast milk or formula under 6 months), dress your baby in one light layer, and let them rest. Don't use alcohol rubs, ice, or cold baths.


### What is a febrile seizure, and is it dangerous?


A seizure caused by a fever, usually between 6 months and 5 years. It is usually under 1 to 2 minutes and almost always harmless. Call 911 if it lasts more than 5 minutes.


### Does a fever cause brain damage?


No. The fever itself does not harm the brain. Serious infections behind a fever, like meningitis, are what can be dangerous - which is why the warning signs matter.


### Does teething cause a true fever?


No. Teething may cause a slight rise within the normal range, but not a true fever of 100.4°F or higher.


### My baby is under 3 months old with a fever - what should I do?


Call your pediatrician right away, even if your baby seems fine. Don't give fever medicine first. See our newborn fever guide for more.


### How long is too long for a baby's fever?


Under 3 months, any fever needs a doctor right away. From 3 months to 2 years, call if a fever lasts more than 24 hours. At 2 and older, more than 3 days. At any age, a fever that comes back after being gone a day is worth a call.
